cases.quote: The following are lists of (non-ideographic) characters from a subset of ISO/IEC 10646 (collection number 285 "BASIC JAPANESE" and 286 "JAPANESE NON IDEOGRAPHICS EXTENSION") grouped by character class according to the classification explained in § 3.9.2 Grouping of Characters and Symbols depending on their Positioning.
cases.rationale: §A.26 is a heading and one table row and nothing else. That row names U+0020 SPACE, and its Character (字形), Common name (通用名称) and Remarks (備考) cells are all empty in both the English and the Japanese rendering, so the first member of cl-26 and its last member are the same member and the class qualifies it by nothing at all: no character frame (字幅), no writing direction, no role. Every substantive sentence about a Western word space in this document lives outside Appendix A, which makes this the class whose Appendix A entry tells a reader almost nothing. The answer therefore turns entirely on the other two tables that name the same key. §A.24 lists 0020 with the Remarks cell "quarter em width" / 「位取りの空白／字幅は四分角」 and §A.25 lists it with the identical cell; those are the only qualifications the document attaches to this key anywhere, and an occurrence declared on the third em is described by neither. §3.9.1 puts the character width first among the axes on which positioning differs, which is why the class may not be answered without reading the declared frame. The third em is JLReq's own geometry for this occurrence — §3.2.2 states that a Western word space is a one third em space in principle — so this is the occurrence supplied by a caller who set the space on the document's own measure. §A.27 does not enter: its 778 rows do not include 0020, so in this document the Western word space is not a Western character. The stream declares an em of 1200 rather than the more usual 1000 because 1200 is divisible by 2, 3, 4 and 5, which are the four denominators the document states for this one class — a half em, a third em, a quarter em and a fifth em — so every advance in this file is exact rather than rounded.

permitted.source: JLReq §A.26, its sole row (U+0020), against the Remarks column of §A.24 and §A.25 (§3.9.1, §3.9.2)

forbidden.why: §A.24 qualifies its listing of 0020 with a quarter em frame, and in its Japanese half with the digit-grouping role 「位取りの空白」. This occurrence declares the third em and no role, so the sentence that would put it in cl-24 does not describe it. §3.9.1 asks "Is the character width full-width, half-width, or something else?" first among the axes on which positioning differs.

§A.27 lists 778 keys and 0020 is not one of them. The Western word space is not a Western character in this document's tables, however Western the text around it is, so the rule that catches every other proportionally-set Latin key does not reach this occurrence.

cases.quote: Is the character width full-width, half-width, or something else?
cases.rationale: The same text as the case above with the word space declared on the frame a real Western font reports for it, and the expected class is byte-identical — which is the assertion. §A.26 states no frame for its one member, so no frame the caller declares can move it, and the two tables that do state a frame for this key state a quarter em, which this occurrence is not either. The obvious wrong answer is cl-27, because a proportionally-set Latin character is cl-27 by §3.2.6 and by §A.27's own Remarks column, and this occurrence sits between four of them; but §A.27 does not list 0020, so the rule that catches every other proportional key leaves this one where §A.26 put it. Read as a pair, the two cases say what ADR 0008 turns on from the other side: here the declared frame decides a geometry and never a class, and an implementation that reads the frame as a class selector answers differently in the two cases while an implementation that reads the tables answers 26 in both and has no work to do.

permitted.source: JLReq §A.26, its sole row (U+0020); §A.27 does not list 0020 (§3.9.1, §3.9.2)

forbidden.why: The answer an implementation gives that decides cl-27 from the proportional frame and the Latin neighbors rather than from the table. §A.27 enumerates 778 keys and 0020 is absent from all of them; §A.26 enumerates one and it is 0020. Widening cl-27 to "whatever a Western font set" empties cl-26 of its only member.

cases.quote: Note that Western word space (cl-26) is a one third em space, in principle, except at line head, line head of warichu, line end and line end of warichu. Western word space (cl-26) at line head, line head of warichu, line end and line end of warichu, is set solid.
cases.rationale: cl-26 has an amount stated for one writing direction and a membership stated for neither, and this case exists so the two are not confused. The sentence quoted above is the only place the one third em default appears, and it sits under the heading "Mixed Text Composition in Horizontal Writing Mode" / 「横組の和欧文混植に用いる文字」; §3.2.3, its vertical counterpart, says nothing about cl-26 and nothing about spaces at all. Meanwhile §B.2 note 13, §D and §E each state their own cl-26 amounts with no direction qualification whatever. So the direction scope belongs to §3.2.2's amount alone. Membership carries none of it: §A.26's Remarks cell is empty, and an empty Remarks cell is where Appendix A records a writing-mode restriction when it has one to record — §A.6's second row carries 「横組で使用」 for U+002E, and §A.26 carries nothing. The case declares the vertical direction and expects the same class as the two horizontal cases above, which is what an implementation that pushed a direction fact from §3.2.2 down into the class layer would get wrong. It would also be the wrong place to fix it: a direction-conditional class would make the class of an occurrence change when the same text is reset, and the document conditions an amount, not a membership.

permitted.source: JLReq §A.26, whose Remarks cell states no writing-mode restriction (§3.9.1, §3.9.2)

forbidden.why: The answer an implementation gives that reasons "vertical composition is Japanese composition, so a space in it is the Japanese space". §A.14 enumerates one key and it is 3000, not 0020; §A.26 enumerates one key and it is 0020. Neither table states a direction.

cases.quote: A few character classes of this document are modified from JIS X 4051. In § A. Character Classes , there is a whole mapping table to ISO/IEC 10646 Annex A collection 285 (BASIC JAPANESE) and collection 286 (JAPANESE NON IDEOGRAPHIC EXTENSION). All character classes of this document are as follows:
cases.rationale: cl-26 holds exactly one key and that key is one code point, and this case is what states it. §A.26's table is one row. Unlike §A.27, which keys twenty-five of its entries on an ordered pair of code points and lists <02E5, 02E9> and <02E9, 02E5> as two distinct members, cl-26 enumerates no code-point sequence at all, so a longest-first scan over Appendix A's key structure has nothing here to join. Two word spaces written side by side — the double space after a sentence that Western manuscript practice still carries — are consequently two occurrences of one key rather than one occurrence of a two-code-point key, and the case asks about the second, which is the occurrence an implementation that glued the pair together would no longer have to answer for. The class is the same as if it stood alone, because §A.26 says nothing about what precedes a member; every statement this document makes about a word space being set solid is about a position on a line, never about a neighbor.

permitted.source: JLReq §A.26, its sole row read twice; the table enumerates no sequence (§3.9.1, §3.9.2)

cases.quote: Sequences of European numerals which are not full-width and are handled as Japanese text, the decimal point or the comma and space used as a decimal place indicator in numbers.
cases.rationale: This is where cl-26 stops, and it is also where the document stops separating. The same key 0020 is listed by §A.24 and by §A.25, and for this key the two Remarks cells are identical character for character: "quarter em width" in English, 「位取りの空白／字幅は四分角」 in Japanese — a quarter em frame and, in the Japanese half alone, the digit-grouping role. That the role is stated in one rendering only is recorded over these very cells as `cl-24-remarks-role-stated-only-in-japanese` in spec/derived/defects.tsv, and the role is read from the half that states it. This occurrence declares both facts, so both qualified listings describe it and §A.26's unqualified row no longer does: an unqualified listing is what remains where no qualified one speaks, which is the same reading of the Remarks column that separates a proportionally-set key from its Japanese listing elsewhere in Appendix A. What the document does not do is separate §A.24 from §A.25, because for 0020 it writes the same qualification in both. The axis that would separate them is the construct the occurrence sits in — §3.9.2 defines cl-24 by the grouped numeral (連数字) and cl-25 by "combinations of Latin script and Greek script characters used for international units (SI)" — and which construct an occurrence belongs to is a fact its caller declares, not one a table decides. This case format has no field for either construct: `constructs` carries ruby, emphasis, tate-chu-yoko, warichu, furiwake, jidori, reference marks, ornaments and formulae, and neither a grouped numeral nor a unit symbol. Both survivors are therefore recorded with the question that chooses between them, rather than one being asserted from the digits standing beside the space. The digits are not what the case asks about; they are what makes the declared role true.

permitted.source: kumihan's published reading of §3.9.2's silence (docs/decisions/ambiguous-context.md), over the survivors §A.24 and §A.25 leave
The other survivor of §A.24 and §A.25, whose Remarks cells for 0020 are identical

forbidden.why: §A.26's row states no frame and no role, so it is the listing that remains where no other describes the occurrence. Here two do: this space declares the quarter em frame and the digit-grouping role that §A.24 and §A.25 both state for key 0020 in so many words. Answering cl-26 for every U+0020 is answering from the code point, and it is the answer of an implementation that read §A.26 and never read §A.24.

cases.quote: However, there are some ambiguous cases, such as "エディター（editor）は……". In this case, English spelling is indicated using parentheses in a Japanese line of text. In this particular case, Japanese design is better.
cases.rationale: U+0020 is named by three Appendix A tables — §A.24, §A.25 and §A.26 — and the only thing separating them is the qualification §A.24 and §A.25 carry in their Remarks cells and §A.26 does not. A caller who declares neither the frame nor the role has supplied nothing that satisfies a qualification and nothing that fails one, so all three listings stand, and the document decides nothing between them: §3.9.2 offers a preference over one example, the Latin spelling parenthesized inside Japanese, and a preference stated about one example is not a rule that names a class. Both ends of the surviving set are therefore recorded rather than one, with the policy question that selects each. Of the three survivors two are membership *in* a construct — §3.9.2 defines cl-24 by the grouped numeral (連数字) and cl-25 by the SI unit symbol — and this caller has declared neither, so this project's published reading takes the lowest-numbered survivor the supplied facts can reach, which is cl-26 (docs/decisions/ambiguous-context.md). The highest-numbered survivor is cl-26 as well: on this key the two ends of the reading coincide once the construct classes are passed over, and both are recorded rather than one so the coincidence is published rather than assumed. The advance is a third em because a caller who has not declared a frame has still measured something, and ADR 0002 forbids reading a frame out of it — a space measured at a third em is exactly as consistent with §A.24's quarter em qualification being unmet as with §A.26's silence.

permitted.source: kumihan's published reading of §3.9.2's silence (docs/decisions/ambiguous-context.md): the lowest-numbered survivor the supplied facts can reach
The highest-numbered survivor of §A.24, §A.25 and §A.26, preferring the Western reading of an undeclared occurrence

forbidden.why: §3.9.2 defines cl-24 as the characters of a grouped numeral (連数字) and names this key by the job it does there, '位取りの空白'. A caller who has declared neither the construct nor the role has said nothing that puts the occurrence inside one, and answering cl-24 states about their document something their document does not.

cases.quote: To work around this issue, many existing implementations use compatibility characters encoded separately in the standard for the purpose of round-trip integrity with the legacy encoding standards. For example, while this document lists U+0028 LEFT PARENTHESIS as a member of opening brackets (cl-01), the compatibility counterpart U+FF08 FULLWIDTH LEFT PARENTHESIS is used in the Japanese context in most Japanese text layout software.
cases.rationale: The sharpest boundary this class has, and it is invisible unless an implementation looks for it. U+3000 IDEOGRAPHIC SPACE carries the Unicode decomposition `<wide> 0020`, so the very folding the Appendix A preamble Note asks for — read the compatibility counterpart as the key this document lists — turns the ideographic space into §A.26's one key if it is applied without a guard, and the folding is not optional: without it a library gives wrong classes on ordinary Japanese text, because the counterparts are what Japanese layout software sets. The guard is that U+3000 is not a counterpart of anything here. It is a listed key in its own right: §A.14 enumerates exactly one member, 3000, under the full-width ideographic space (和字間隔, cl-14), and a fold that consumed it would leave a class §3.9.2 closes at thirty with no member at all. The document holds the two apart in one sentence of §3.7.3 — "Where Western word space (cl-26) or full-width ideographic space (cl-14) are inserted" / 「欧文間隔（cl-26），和字間隔（cl-14）など空白を挿入してある箇所」 — which it could not write if either folded onto the other. An implementation that normalizes its input before classifying, by NFKC or by any full-width-to-half-width pass, answers cl-26 here, and thereby gives every full-width space in a Japanese paragraph the class the document reserves for the space between two Western words, with the first stage of both line-adjustment ladders attached to it.

permitted.source: JLReq §A.14, its sole row (U+3000), which §A.26's key does not reach (§3.9.2)

forbidden.why: The answer produced by folding a Wide decomposition onto a code point Appendix A already lists. §A.14 names 3000 as the one member of cl-14 and §A.26 names 0020 as the one member of cl-26; a fold that reads the first as the second empties cl-14 and doubles the membership of cl-26. §A's preamble Note licenses reading a compatibility counterpart as the key the document lists, and U+3000 is a key the document lists.

cases.quote: Western characters (cl-27) include punctuation marks, such as commas, used in Western context. Among these punctuation marks, several marks are used both in a Japanese context and Western context.
cases.rationale: The character that is a Western word space in every sense except this document's. U+00A0 NO-BREAK SPACE is what a Western compositor writes where a word space must not become a break, and JLReq does not put it in cl-26: §A.26's table has one row and it is 0020. §A.27 lists it — Common name 「ノーブレークスペース」, Remarks "proportionally-spaced" / 「プロポーショナル」 — and it is the only table in the whole of Appendix A that names the key, so cl-27 is the answer with nothing further to consult, and this occurrence satisfies the one qualification §A.27 attaches to it. The distinction is not cosmetic. cl-26 is named as the first stage of line adjustment in both directions, by §3.2.6, §3.8.3 and §3.8.4, and cl-27 is not; so an implementation that widens §A.26 from a code point to a notion of "word space" has made the one space the author wrote in order to forbid a break into the first thing its justifier stretches and squeezes. That an unbreakable space and a breakable one are two classes is the document being consistent, not the document being terse.

permitted.source: JLReq §A.27's row for 00A0, Remarks "proportionally-spaced"; no other table names the key (§3.9.1, §3.9.2)

forbidden.why: §A.26 enumerates one key, 0020, and 00A0 is not it. Classifying by what a space is for rather than by the tables puts a character whose whole purpose is to forbid a break into the class the document drains first during line adjustment.

cases.quote: JIS X 4051 also provides similar  character classes but that are slightly different from this document. Furthermore JIS X 4051 states that it is implementation-defined how to handle characters that are not explicitly mentioned, e.g. whether they should belong to either class or not.
cases.rationale: The other side of the same boundary: a space Appendix A does not name at all. U+2002 EN SPACE is a fixed-width word space of Western typography and no table in Appendix A lists it. Its absence is a scope statement rather than an oversight — the appendix's preamble bounds its tables to the non-ideographic characters of ISO/IEC 10646 collections 285 and 286 — and §3.9.2 records that JIS X 4051 leaves a character it does not mention implementation-defined, and does not replace that. So cl-26 is exactly one code point and not the category "spaces": an implementation that widened §A.26 into a category answers cl-26 here and has invented a member of a class whose whole enumeration is one row. What this project answers instead is a published reading and not a requirement, which is why the standing is `unstated` and both readings appear below with the question that selects each. The reading extends the one distinction JLReq itself draws over text its tables do not enumerate: §3.2.4 sets full-width and fixed-width Western characters as quasi Japanese characters and §3.2.6 gives proportionally-set Western text the composition rules of cl-27, so the frame the caller declared is what decides, and this occurrence declares the proportional one. The alternative answers the ideographic class for every unlisted key whatever its frame. Recorded in docs/decisions/unlisted-code-point.md.

permitted.source: kumihan's published reading of §3.9.2's silence (docs/decisions/unlisted-code-point.md), by the frame §3.2.6 makes decisive
The alternative reading of the same silence: the ideographic class for every unlisted key, whatever its frame

forbidden.why: §A.26 enumerates one key and it is 0020. Answering cl-26 for a code point the appendix never names is not a reading of a silence but an addition to a closed table, and it would give a fixed-width en space the reducible and expandable behavior the document states for a word space that a compositor may resize.
